title: Krishna, the Lord himself
hookLine: one small word in the Bhagavata, and two schools that read it with love
carry: krishna is the lord himself: one verse, two schools
tomorrow: Arjuna asks Krishna: how can you be that old? what's the answer?
last: HIDDEN, AND CARRIED THROUGH THE RAIN.

lines: A COMMA CAN END A FRIENDSHIP.
cards: Whole group chats have melted down over a comma. Let's eat, Grandma, is dinner; drop the comma and it's a horror movie. Small marks carry big meanings.
The Bhagavata Purana has its own small mark. Its first book lists Vishnu's descents like a roll call: the fish, the boar, the man-lion, the dwarf, Rama, sages and kings among them.
Right after the list comes one short line, with one small word in it: tu, which means but. Two schools of Krishna's devotees read that but in two different ways.

teach.b: Here's the line, in Sanskrit: krishnas tu bhagavan svayam.
All the names above, the verse says, are portions, or parts of portions, of the Supreme Person. But Krishna is Bhagavan himself, the Lord in person. Now let both readings speak.
Gaudiya Vaishnavas, who follow the teacher Chaitanya, hear the but as a hinge. Krishna isn't one descent among many.
He's the source the others come from, and the verse says so in plain words; reading past it would be strange.
Other Vaishnava schools, Sri Vaishnavas and the followers of Madhva among them, hear Krishna as a full descent of Vishnu, or Narayana, who stays the source.

For them the verse honors Krishna as complete, not partial, without lifting him out of Vishnu's line. And they can point to yesterday's birth scene, where the newborn first appears in Vishnu's four-armed form.
Both readings keep every name on the list. Both bow to Krishna.

teach.h: WHICH WAY DOES THE ARROW POINT?
teach.b: What they part on is which way the arrow points: from Krishna to Vishnu, or from Vishnu to Krishna.
And that's a big part of how Hinduism lives: one scripture, many sampradayas, living lines of teachers, each reading with care. Neither side throws the verse away.
They argue over it because it matters, and that's a kind of respect.

how: Gaudiya Vaishnava teachers often cite krishnas tu bhagavan svayam when they explain Krishna as the source of the avatars; Sri Vaishnava and Madhva teachers read Krishna as a descent of Vishnu or Narayana.

o: the one the Bhagavata calls the Lord himself
the poet who first wrote down the Bhagavata
a sage named on the Bhagavata's list of descents

games.q: one verse, two readings — tap the pairs.
p: but: the small word in the middle
Krishna is the source of the others

s: the Bhagavata's first list of descents stops at exactly ten
its first list runs longer, with sages and kings among the names.
the verse says the others are portions, but Krishna is the Lord himself
that's krishnas tu bhagavan svayam, Bhagavata 1.3.28.
every Vaishnava school reads that verse the same way
Gaudiya Vaishnavas read Krishna as the source; other schools read him as Vishnu's full descent.

games.q: Sam asks you to argue the side you don't hold. say you read Krishna as Vishnu's descent. what's the Gaudiya side's strongest case?
o: the verse's own words: the others are portions, but Krishna is the Lord in person.
Krishna has more stories and festivals, so he must be the bigger one.
Krishna came later in the list, so he replaced Vishnu as the main god.
games.why: a fair argument uses the other side's best evidence. For Gaudiya Vaishnavas, that's the verse itself: krishnas tu bhagavan svayam.

practice: Say the line out loud once, slowly: krishnas tu bhagavan svayam. Say it a second time and lean on tu, the but, then breathe in the pause it leaves for the rest of the sit.
If saying Sanskrit isn't part of your practice, hold the English instead: but Krishna is the Lord himself.

wordCard.voice: Krishna: in the Bhagavata's line, the one named not a portion but the Lord himself, read as the source by some and as Vishnu's full descent by others.

orig.note: Sanskrit svayam: himself, in person, the last word of krishnas tu bhagavan svayam.
